column1: What perceptual phenomenon allows discrete still frames to be perceived as continuous motion in stop motion animation?
column2: Persistence of vision combined with the phi phenomenon—the retina retains images for ~1/15th second and the brain interpolates sequential static frames into continuous motion above a perceptual threshold frequency.

column1: Why is 24fps the optimal standard frame rate for Lego stop motion, rather than higher rates like 60fps?
column2: 24fps matches broadcast/streaming delivery standards and provides sufficient temporal resolution to render Lego's discrete geometry as organic motion, while gains above 30fps diminish rapidly even as shooting time and storage scale linearly with each added frame.

column1: What happens below 12fps and what is this effect called?
column2: Below ~12fps, the discrete nature of individual frames becomes perceptually obvious, producing a stroboscopic flicker effect rather than smooth motion.

column1: What is 'easing' in animation, and what are its three main types?
column2: Easing is graduated frame spacing that mimics biological acceleration/deceleration: ease-in (accelerating from rest), ease-out (decelerating to rest), and ease-in-out (both), producing naturalistic weight versus uniform/mechanical motion.

column1: Why does uniform (linear) spacing between frames look unnatural for character animation?
column2: Uniform spacing produces constant velocity motion, which is mechanical and robotic because it lacks the inertia-driven acceleration/deceleration profile inherent to biological movement.

column1: What is Lego 'clutch power' and what force range does it typically occupy for a 2x4 brick on studs?
column2: Clutch power is the friction-based interference fit resistance to separation between a brick and studs, typically approximately 50 to 80 Newtons, varying by part family, color, and manufacturing batch.

column1: Why do white and light gray Lego bricks often exhibit lower clutch power than other colors?
column2: Calcium carbonate additives used to achieve opacity in white and light gray ABS formulations reduce the friction coefficient, measurably lowering clutch power.

column1: What is the fundamental Lego grid constraint governing standard connection spacing, and why does it matter for stop motion?
column2: All standard Lego connections occur at integer multiples of 7.8mm horizontally and 9.6mm vertically (5:6 aspect ratio), forcing discrete positional jumps unless sub-stud techniques (brackets, hinges, SNOT) are used for gradual motion.

column1: What range of motion does a standard Lego minifigure hip joint permit?
column2: Approximately 90 degrees of forward flexion and 45 degrees of lateral abduction, with no rotation about the longitudinal axis.

column1: Why must camera aperture be stopped down to f/8 or narrower when shooting Lego minifigures, and what tradeoff does this create?
column2: At minifigure macro scale (~4cm tall), depth of field collapses to a fraction of a millimeter at wide apertures; narrowing to f/8+ restores a usable focal plane but demands significantly higher light intensity to properly expose the shot.

column1: What Pythagorean truss configuration is recommended for a Lego camera boom, and why?
column2: A 5-12-13 Pythagorean truss built from Technic liftarms with diagonal cross-bracing resists vertical bending/torsional sag, preventing camera drift between frames caused by structural deflection under load.

column1: What is the maximum acceptable lighting intensity variation (in stops) across frames to avoid visible flicker in stop motion?
column2: Lighting must remain stable within ±0.3 stops of intensity across the exposure sequence to avoid perceptible flicker in the compiled animation.
